As a Tamilian I found the perspective on lack of spiritual emptiness and cultural grounding interesting. While I dont deny the fact that you will find a lot of people who treat stars like gods here, you notice a lot of stars previously have tried to enter politics and failed as well. So stardom and fandom might have played a huge role in Vijay’s victory, but there’s more to it. The DMK and ADMK are the status quo parties ruling for over 60+ years. Anti- establishment sentiments, the shear arragance of the ruling party representatives, a bought out media, dynastic politics ( in DMK), high levels of corruption among both the existing parties, rising cases of violence against women and drug addiction among the youth were other key issues. 

In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, the BJP under Annamalai although did not win any seats, had secured an impressive vote share of 18%. That brought to light that there was a large and growing section of the population who wanted another alternative to the Dravidian parties. Unfortunately the BJP made the mistake to remove Annamalai from the political scene after 2024. 

I personally dont agree with the spiritual emptiness argument fully. I was born and brought up in Chennai for a majority of my early childhood. Tamil Nadu is one of the most Hindu states in India, the shear number of temples and utmost devotion can be seen here, I am witness to it. But I have grown among friends from different religions and we were taught to respect each other irrespective of religion. So we naturally separate religious identity and rhetoric from political rhetoric. The same cannot be said about caste however.

The positives from this election were that a political party can win without bribing the voters with 500 and 1000 rupees per vote which the other parties did. Candidates won irrespective of their caste, religion or gender, they broke the usual political calculus of caste based votes. A lot of young, albeit inexperienced,  and educated people have entered the Legislative Assembly, reducing the average age to 40, this is a welcome change. But they do need to learn the way things work in administration.

In essence, this verdict brought in a new political experiment in TN. Whether its a failure or success, only time will tell.

comments.text:
People in this comment section are acting way too toxic instead of having an actual political discussion. Many people supporting TVK and Vijay are not blindly voting for an actor — they supported him because they were frustrated with the same political cycle in Tamil Nadu for decades.

Both DMK and AIADMK ruled for years, yet people still complained about corruption, dynasty politics, poor infrastructure planning in many areas, rising drug issues among youngsters, and politicians focusing more on party fights than real public development. That frustration is exactly why so many people searched for a different alternative.

And about the Karur conference deaths — blaming Vijay personally for every tragedy is unfair and politically motivated.
Many people themselves pointed out issues related to poor arrangements, crowd management failures, and local corruption. When similar incidents happen in rallies of older parties, nobody says people are “dying for politicians,” but when it comes to Vijay, suddenly the narrative changes.

Tamil Nadu people are educated enough to think and decide for themselves. South India has consistently performed better in education, healthcare, and social development compared to many northern states, so stop acting like voters here are ignorant or emotional voters. Vijay’s support was never just cinema fandom — for many youngsters and middle-class families, he became a symbol of change and a break from the same DMK vs AIADMK politics.
And now people are already seeing the difference in attitude. Vijay himself said he doesn’t want unnecessary traffic and public inconvenience just because he goes outside for lunch, so he would rather bring food and work like a normal government employee from morning till evening. These small things matter because people are tired of VIP culture and politicians acting above the public. Whether you support him or not, at least respect why so many people in Tamil Nadu wanted this change.

And yes, there are definitely some overexcited fans who do cringe things like extreme tattoos, dramatic celebrations, or weird behavior outside celebritie's houses. Even many Vijay supporters themselves don’t support that kind of fan culture. But judging an entire political movement or every voter based on a few extreme fans is completely unfair. Every major party and every big celebrity in India has toxic supporters — that doesn’t represent all the normal people who support them for genuine political reasons. Most TVK supporters are ordinary people who simply wanted change in Tamil Nadu politics, not blind fanatics.

I loved this video. Every point covered perfectly!

One thing that really frustrates me is how some people from Kerala and Tamil Nadu flex their literacy rates and try to portray North Indians as uneducated or foolish. Ironically, the same attitude is often shown towards Telugu states and Telugu people by the rest of South India.

I'm honestly tired of seeing Telugu people constantly targeted on social media, as if only Telugu audiences engage in hero worship. People bring up the literacy rates of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, use that as an excuse to mock Telugu people, and even throw around so-called insults like "Bihar of South India." Criticizing toxic hero worship is completely fine, but what is unacceptable is the constantly trying to generalize an entire community while pretending to be morally and intellectually superior, despite similar behavior existing everywhere.

In reality, extreme hero worship in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana is mostly concentrated in certain caste-based fan club cultures, mainly among sections of Kamma and Kapu communities, which together form only a part of the population. It does not represent every Telugu person. (btw Sham pronounced Kamma and Kapu correctly unlike the previous video, so kudos for rectifying it)

The political culture of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu is also very different. In Tamil Nadu, many actors enter cinema with political ambitions from the beginning. In Andhra Pradesh, actors usually enter politics much later in life.

Take N. T. Rama Rao for example. He entered politics at a time when Andhra Pradesh had no strong regional party and Congress dominated the state. Chief Ministers were frequently changed based on directions from Delhi, and many Telugu people felt that the Centre neither respected nor cared about Telugu identity and interests. SR. NTR launched his party with the slogan "Telugu Vari Atma Gauravam" (self-respect of Telugu people). Within just 8 months of founding the party, he achieved a historic electoral victory. This was in 1983, long before social media or organized fan culture as we know it today. His success was not simply because of fan clubs, but because people connected with his message and leadership.

Pawan Kalyan did not have an easy life despite being the brother of megastar Chiranjeevi. He struggled with serious health issues and depression during his younger years and even went through suicidal thoughts at one point. Despite having massive popularity in cinema, he repeatedly considered leaving the film industry altogether. He entered politics not for immediate power, but because he genuinely wanted to work for people. He spent nearly 10 years building his political journey before eventually becoming Deputy Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh. He won zero seats in his first election. Whether people agree with his politics or not, it is unfair to dismiss his journey as mere "hero worship." A lot of hard work, persistence, and personal struggle went into it. The journey of Pawan Kalyan and Vijay is not even comparable.

Criticize unhealthy fan culture wherever necessary, but people should stop stereotyping all Telugu people as foolish or backward. Every state has its strengths, weaknesses, and forms of celebrity culture.
